fatal_errors: The proposed doped TiO2 coating is not supported by either cited source; neither source studies a doped TiO2 self-healing coating on CoCrFeNi.
The intervention does not reconstruct the target strategy of varying Mo content in a CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 bulk composite.
The starting material is incorrectly treated as bare CoCrFeNi rather than the specified multicomponent powder composite.
The coating composition, dopant, deposition method, thickness, adhesion requirements, and low-temperature lubrication mechanism are unspecified.
The proposed falsification rule emphasizes temperatures above 600 °C and therefore does not test the claim of low friction and wear throughout the full room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad wide-temperature tribology problem and proposes a controlled coated-versus-uncoated comparison, but it is neither a reconstruction of the target intervention nor an evidence-grounded alternative as written. Its glaze-layer concept qualitatively resembles the target's high-temperature adaptive tribofilm mechanism, yet it omits the Mo-induced lattice distortion and sigma-phase strengthening, low-temperature MoS2/Ag lubrication, and high-temperature silver-molybdate chemistry. Conditions are too vague: no definite load, speed, distance, counterface, coating specification, or thermal-cycling protocol is given. E1 supports adaptive interfaces in a different bulk Ni-based alloy, while E2 supports oxidation resistance of an AlCrTiZrMo HEA film; neither validates TiO2, self-healing behavior, or low shear across the full range. The experiment could distinguish coated from uncoated behavior, but it needs a fully specified coating, the target test conditions, replicated measurements at every temperature, and a falsification criterion requiring improvement across the entire regime.
